title.narrative: NIGER-NIGERIA REPORT OF THE FINAL EVALUATION OF STRENGTHENING NIGER-NIGERIA COOPERATION ON COUNTERING TRAFFICKING IN HUMAN BEINGS

description.narrative:
Strengthening Niger and Nigeria Cooperation on Countering Trafficking in Human Beings Final Evaluation Conducted by Mr. Silviu Kondan and Ms. Rowena Symss
PROJECT DESCRIPTION Name of ProjectStrengthening Niger and Nigeria Cooperation on Countering Trafficking in Human Beings (NG-NR project) Implementing agencyInternational Centre for Migration Policy Development (ICMPD) DonorKingdom of the Netherlands Beneficiary (Direct)The National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP) in Nigeria The National Agency for the Fight against Trafficking in Persons and the Illicit Transport of Migrants (ANLTP/TIM) in Niger Project Duration24 Months; January, 1 2021 – December 31, 2022 NCE granted to June 30, 2023 Budget€1,590,945.00 Project Manager:Ms. Mojisola Sodeinde Project ObjectiveTo strengthen the institutional response to trafficking in human beings in Niger and Nigeria, through enhanced bilateral cooperation
DESCRIPTION OF THE INTERVENTION Strengthening Niger-Nigeria Cooperation on Countering Trafficking in Human Beings (NG-NR) Niger and Nigeria, both being Member States of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and sharing a border that spans approximately 1500 kilometers, are located within the ECOWAS free movement zone – granted under the Protocol on the Free Movement of Persons, Right of Residence and Establishment. Within this context, Niger primarily serves as a transit point for many West Africans who subsequently seek to travel to Europe. This includes a significant number of Nigerians who pass through Niger. Nigeria, on the other hand, serves as a source, transit, and destination country for migration. Nigerians' susceptibility to trafficking is heightened by factors such as poverty, uneven and limited economic prospects, corruption, widespread insecurity across specific regions of the country, and the pressure to migrate due to effects of climate change and population growth. Consequently, a considerable portion of Nigerians engage in irregular migration to Southern Europe vis-à-vis the North Africa-Mediterranean route. These irregular migrants often rely on human smuggling networks across Niger and North Africa (especially Algeria, Libya and Morocco), and unfortunately, are susceptible to falling victim to trafficking. For example, some of these migrants have fallen prey to trafficking and find themselves stranded in transit cities like Agadez, Arlit, and Dirkou – and in certain cases, reports of sexual exploitation have emerged, particularly affecting young women from Nigeria. In 2021, Algeria expelled over 27,000 refugees and migrants, including Nigerien and foreign nationals, to Niger. Again, between January and May of 2022, 14,000 migrants were expelled from Algeria to Niger– leading to increased vulnerability amongst migrants displaced across Niger. It is also important to note that human traffickers also exploit domestic victims in Niger. According to the 2022 trafficking in persons (TIP) report for Niger, hereditary and caste-based slavery practices continue to be perpetrated by politically influential community leaders. While estimates of the numbers of persons exploited in modern-day slavery vary widely, one report estimates it is as high as 800,000. This form of trafficking mainly involves the exploitation of Nigerien children and women, as well as victims from West and Central African countries, in both sex and labor trafficking. Semi-organized transnational criminal groups are known to exploit children from Niger and neighboring countries in various sectors, such as mining (gold, salt, trona, and gypsum mines), agriculture, forced begging, stone quarries, markets, bus stations, and manufacturing within the country. In some cases, girls who flee from forced marriages are particularly vulnerable to traffickers, who exploit them in commercial sex, as they lack access to support services. Past incidents have revealed that a lack of proper protection measures for victims of trafficking (VOTs) can severely hinder their cooperation with law enforcement, impeding the successful prosecution and conviction of traffickers. Nigerien authorities often face difficulties in engaging with Nigerian victims due to various reasons such as trauma, lack of trust, language barriers, and more. Thus, it is crucial to adopt a victim-centered approach and develop innovative methods to collaborate with victims throughout the criminal proceedings, despite these challenges. With direct financial support from the Kingdom of the Netherlands, the International Centre for Migration Policy Development (ICMPD) is supporting both countries through the NG-NR project, and more directly the National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons and other Related Matters (NAPTIP) in Nigeria and the National Agency for the Fight against Trafficking in Persons and the Illicit Transport of Migrants (ANLTP/TIM) in Niger. The Kingdom of the Netherlands considers Niger and Nigeria as countries of significant interest for various reasons. Nigeria is recognized as one of the top countries of origin for trafficked victims and asylum seekers in the Netherlands, with Niger serving as a transit point for many of them. The NG-NR project was designed by ICMPD out of a need to address institutional gaps that could be more directly resolved vis-à-vis bilateral cooperation. The overall objective of the project was precisely “to strengthen the institutional response to Trafficking in Human Beings in Niger and Nigeria, through enhanced bilateral cooperation.” More specifically, the project sought to establish a cooperation platform to promote the exchange of information on trafficking; to facilitate collaboration in the investigation and dismantling of criminal networks; to support the harmonization of tools and procedures for combating trafficking; and to develop and implement an enabling framework for the assistance and protection of VOTs and potential victims in both countries. The original work plan for the NG-NR project spanned 24 months (January 1, 2021 – December 31, 2022). However, due to a number of internal and external constraints, including with the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, the project obtained two no-cost extensions (NCE) until June 30, 2023, to appropriately adjust project activities and timelines. Description of Project Beneficiaries Beneficiaries The primary beneficiaries of this intervention were the NAPTIP and ANLTP/TIM. Secondary beneficiaries, who were less directly affected by project results, include migrants, community members and other actors mandated to address TIP.
A collaborative technical working group – the Joint Technical Working Group (JTWG) was established to facilitate coordination between the national TIP agencies to streamline coordination efforts in addressing TIP between the two countries. Subsequently, four sub-committees were established to identify common priorities and implement jointly coordinated interventions: Investigation & Prosecution, Prevention, Protection & Repatriation and Partnership & Resource Mobilization. The JTWG and the four sub-committees are comprised of various representatives from government agencies and a number of selected non-governmental organizations (NGOs) responsible with combatting a specific aspect of TIP, including: ●Agence Nationale de Lutte contre la Traite des Personnes (ANLTP/TIM), Niger ●Coordinating Commission for the Fight against Trafficking in Persons (CNCLTP), Niger ●Direction de la Surveillance du Territoire (DST), Niger ●Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Niger ●Ministry of Foreign Affairs, Nigeria ●Federal Ministry of Humanitarian Services Disaster Management and Social Development, Nigeria ●Ministry of Justice, Niger ●Ministry of Justice, Nigeria ●National Agency for the Prohibition of Trafficking in Persons (NAPTIP), Nigeria ●National Police Force, Nigeria ●Network of Civil Society Organization Against Child Trafficking, Abuse and Labour (NACTAL), Nigeria ●Nigeria Immigration Service (NIS), Nigeria ●ONG Lutte Contre le Trafic Humain et la Prostitution (LTHP), Niger ●Other participants include diplomatic mission representatives from each country, and in certain cases the Dutch diplomatic missions
The following high-level objectives guide each sub-committee: ●Investigation & Prosecution: ○i. Discuss bilateral mechanism/modalities and tools to facilitate joint intelligence sharing, investigation and prosecution of human traffickers and other TIP - related criminal matters along the border corridor based on annual work plan. ○ii. Capacity building on tactical planning session for joint sting operation in reinforcing bilateral cooperation an expert will facilitate sessions to provide support and guidance. ○Planned activities include: organize capacity building trainings on joint investigation and the sharing of intelligence, implementation of a joint sting operation to arrest perpetrators, the procurement of equipment to support investigations, etc. ●Prevention: ○i. Design, develop and implement activities in line with the spirit and letters of the partnership to enhance the prevention of TIP from each of the countries to the other in particular, and preventing the crime in both countries generally. ○ii. Provide tools/instruments to increase both national coordination and bilateral/cross - border cooperation to address and combat TIP. ○iii. Develop mechanisms and interventions among law enforcement agencies, community and religious leaders, etc. along the border corridors of both countries. ○Planned activities include: conducting joint sensitization field mission, facilitate capacity building trainings for law enforcement agencies, communities and religious leaders, etc. ●Protection & Repatriation: ○To establish new shelters for victims of trafficking in Agadez and Niamey. ○To build the capacity of first line responders and their roles in identification, care, reception, rehabilitation and reintegration of victims. ○Planned activities include: organize capacity building initiative(s) on victim needs, trauma counseling and shelter management, develop a bilateral referral mechanism for victims, etc. ●Partnership & Resource Mobilization: ○i. Reflect on the current state of bilateral partnership between Niger and Nigeria. ○ii. Develop plans for resource mobilization for long term sustainability of the cooperation when the sponsors withdraw. ○Planned activities include: organize annual conferences on lessons learned related to combating TIP, facilitate quarterly meetings on behalf of the JTWG, etc.
ICMPD is responsible for managing the overall project and in guiding the strategic planning and implementation of activities. The JTWG included key stakeholders from each country who are responsible for anti-trafficking efforts, who benefit from overcoming existing constraints and barriers through bilateral cooperation. Furthermore, an initial baseline assessment was conducted to assess existing TIP-related frameworks within the national contexts, to evaluate past cooperation efforts and to guide future activities. To further support the two agencies, practical tools were developed and shared with professionals in both countries, providing relevant information on cross-border referral of VOTs and to improve cooperation on criminal matters. Overall, the JTWG serves as a coordination platform for both countries and is responsible for developing an annual work plan with clear objectives, activities and expected results. Project activities are also discussed at the JTWG level, to ensure necessary buy-in and ownership by both TIP agencies.
EVALUATION SCOPE, METHODS & DATA ANALYSIS Purpose and Scope of Evaluation The evaluation of the NG-NR project utilized a set of standardized evaluation criteria categories, which were developed and promoted by the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development - Development Assistance Committee (OECD-DAC). These categories encompassed an assessment of the project's relevance, coherence, effectiveness, efficiency, impact, and sustainability. Additionally, the evaluators analyzed how the project design and implementation integrated principles related to human rights, equity, and gender pluralism as additional cross-cutting themes.
Based on the above-mentioned criteria and the objective of the NG-NR project, this evaluation provides an assessment of the project’s results and outcomes. The findings available from this evaluation will be used to better inform the design and implementation of future phases of the project as well as similar interventions pursued by ICMPD and relevant stakeholders, and to facilitate transparency and accountability with the project donor.
It is important to note that the project team was granted an additional 3-month NCE following the completion of the final evaluation in April 2023. During this time, between May 2023 – June 2023, additional progress toward the project results were achieved. These achievements were reported to the evaluators but were not included in the data collection and analysis process for the final evaluation. As such, the evaluation findings, lessons learned and recommendations are based on the project’s progress until April 2023.
Evaluation Criteria and High-Level Evaluation Questions The following criteria table provides a preliminary and non-exhaustive list of high-level questions and data collection indicators that the consultants developed and referenced throughout the evaluation process.
Figure 1. OECD-DAC Standard Evaluation Criteria and NG-NR I Evaluation Indicators CriteriaDefinitionFinal Evaluation Indicators RelevanceExtent to which the activity was suited to the priorities and policies of the target group, recipient(s) and donor●Extent of alignment to outlined donor priorities ●Demonstrated consideration for relevant needs in project design ●Degree of consultation with partners and beneficiaries and adherence to needs and priorities ●Examples of ways gender pluralism, equity and human rights were considered and incorporated into the project CoherenceCompatibility of the intervention with other interventions in a country, sector or institution●Alignment to international norms and standards ●Examples of internal and external coherence EffectivenessExtent to which the intervention achieved, or is expected to achieve, its objectives, and its results●Achievement of project outputs and attainment of immediate results EfficiencyExtent to which the intervention delivered, or is likely to deliver, results in an economic and timely way●Demonstrated successes and areas of improvement in project planning, implementation and management ●Alignment to planned project budget and schedule ●Quality of M&E tools and processes ImpactPositive and negative changes produced by an intervention, directly or indirectly, intended or unintended●Early indication of long-lasting results (e.g., changes in daily operations or establishment of norms and mechanisms) SustainabilityExtent to which the net benefits of the intervention continue, or are likely to continue●Documentation and sharing of lessons learned ●Likelihood for sustaining and continuing NG-NR project benefits
Data Collection Procedures and Instruments
Figure 2. Planned Outline of Data Collection Methods Proposed by Consultants Data Collection ToolDetailed Activities 1. Desk Review The consultants examined various documents, as provided by the NG-NR project focal contact(s). This included M&E data (meeting minutes, results monitoring framework, key performance indicators/output data), the mid-term evaluation report, project plans, progress and narrative reports, etc. Other sources that the consultants cross-referenced included external publications on the topic of TIP, particularly across the ECOWAS region (e.g., similar project evaluations from IOM, UNODC, etc.).
2. Beneficiary Survey QuestionnaireThe questionnaire acted as the primary input tool for project beneficiaries as well as certain project partners. The tool was structured around the OECD-DAC criteria areas with both quantitative and qualitative question options. The NG-NR project manager shared the survey widely with project beneficiaries.
The consultants included a number of logic branching questions to assess satisfaction and results of specific project components. Respondents completed the corresponding component questions only if the questions relate to their involvement with the NG-NR project.
2. Semi-Structured 1:1 InterviewsIn-depth interviews were conducted with a wide range of stakeholders – including the NG-NR project team, key partners and subject matter experts. The consultants coordinated with the NG-NR project assistant to establish a register of contacts/stakeholders that were important and relevant to interview.
A combination of semi-structured discussions and follow-up validation exchanges were planned. The interview questions were adjusted depending on the stakeholder/informant(s) being interviewed. This was to obtain in-depth insights into the experiences, perceptions, expectations, satisfaction and challenges that each stakeholder group faced. The semi-structured questionnaires were developed to align with the OECD-DAC criteria and to reflect the objectives of the evaluation stated above. 3. Focus Group Sessions with Key InformantsTo aid the data collection process and to promote a participatory approach to the evaluation, the external evaluators organized a series of focus group sessions with the direct project beneficiaries during the 6th JTWG meeting in Niamey during the last week of February 2023. National representatives were present during these sessions, representing members of both national TIP agencies: NAPTIP and ANLTP/TIM as well as civil society actors.
The focus group sessions were developed to correspond with the OECD-DAC criteria categories, with an emphasis on sustainability planning and taking stock of lessons learned. Participants were also invited to connect with the external evaluators separately, to provide any additional feedback on the final evaluation.
FINDINGS ACROSS SELECTED CRITERIA AREAS
Demonstrated consideration for relevant needs in project design
The evaluators believe that the project team benefited from a thorough needs assessment process at the inception of the project, as well as through periodic reviews of project objectives and activities. The NG-NR project team facilitated the initial assessment of priorities by consulting with representatives from both national TIP agencies. These consultations were further formalized into a baseline assessment, conducted in June 2021 by an external team of consultants, to gain a deeper understanding of institutional priorities and gaps. The four thematic areas, reflecting the work of the four sub-committees (i.e., Investigation & Prosecution, Prevention, Protection & Repatriation and Partnership & Resource Mobilization), were strategically selected by the agencies due to their relevance in addressing TIP and building cohesion amongst the two agencies.
According to the focus group participants and corroborated by the semi-structured interviews, there are several gaps, challenges and barriers to combating TIP that were initially identified in the project design, or that were taken stock of throughout the implementation of the project. The project activities, were therefore, developed to cover several operational priorities: trainings offered to front-line actors, capacity-building through the development of cooperation frameworks, awareness raising amongst communities, planning for longer-term sustainability, and encouraging joint-security operations – to name a few.
Although many of the identified gaps, challenges, and barriers related to TIP are seen as requiring long-term bilateral cooperation that extends beyond the first phase of the project, informants from the JTWG sub-committees expressed optimism that enhanced collaboration and bilateral cooperation will ultimately lead to more effective management of TIP-related issues in the long run. The following list captures input on gaps, challenges and/or barriers that are i) in the process of being addressed as a result of the project’s establishment, including the launch of the JTWG and sub-committees and ii) longer-term issues that will require ongoing cooperation and sustainable programming.
Shorter-term issues being addressed through Ng-NR project activities/actions: ●cross-border information sharing systems that are secure, particularly around common border corridors and pathways (incl. airport inspection of fraudulent identity documents – e.g., the use of Nigerian passports); ●lack of familiarization of contacts and structures between the two national TIP agencies, including counterpart contacts to support appropriate information sharing, the ongoing provision of social protection and clear guidelines on return, readmission and reintegration; ●safeguards and protection to victims, vulnerable migrants and informants who provide critical information on perpetrators; ●ongoing professional trainings with learning progressions for front-line agents to better identify both VOTs and suspected perpetrators; ●low awareness amongst community populations about what constitutes a crime and the complexity and drivers of TIP, leading to a lack of identification of VOTs and reporting of crimes.
Longer-term actions requiring the continuation of foundational structures/communication supports (and likely requiring future phasing of NG-NR): ●surveillance and intelligence deployed across vulnerable border regions, including sufficient funding for investigation and prosecution processes and for technical services/infrastructure; ●standardized data collection and sharing between agencies in both countries (i.e., more reliable and valid data on TIP), including subset of irregular migrants who are documented through various checkpoints or who re-engage in irregular migration; ●lack of trust amongst VOTs toward law enforcement during identification processes (incl. misconception about criminalization and protection measures offered to VOTs) as well as fear-based and violent tactics used by perpetrators.
Given the extensive TIP-related issues mentioned above, there were budgetary and human resource constraints to address all noted challenges. The ambitious expectations of national actors had not always been sufficiently met, given the limits to the overall project budget. For example, according to a few focus group informants, the proposed activities included high costs related to requests for technological equipment to improve geolocation-related activities. These activities were de-prioritized as the ICMPD focal team and the Partnership & Resource Mobilization Sub-Committee were unable to feasibly allocate funds to cover these costs.
The evaluators note that the project was designed in a process-oriented manner to create opportunities for national actors to lead activities and to learn from one another. To support this process, ICMPD has provided administrative, project management and thematic support. This has led to the establishment of frameworks (i.e., formal agreement and memorandum of understanding (MOU)) between the agencies, which are designed to lead to continued cooperation after the project concludes. However, the extent to which these frameworks will promote continued engagement amongst the two national agencies is inconclusive, with informants emphasizing the need to foster this engagement and facilitate bilateral cooperation.
Degree of consultation with partners and beneficiaries and adherence to needs and priorities
According to several informants (n=4), there was pre-existing interest amongst national stakeholders to improve TIP mechanisms across the region. For example, the “Support to Free Movement of Persons and Migration in West Africa” (FMM West Africa) project, implemented under a consortium by the International Organization for Migration (IOM) with ongoing support from ICMPD, exposed the need for formalized cooperation between NAPTIP and ANLTP/TIM. During the implementation of FMM, wherein a national referral mechanism for VOTs was developed in Niger and a variety of training tools were developed for NAPTIP, it became evident that coherence between the two agencies was needed as migratory influxes were complicated and required bilateral cooperation. At the same time, the two national TIP agencies required dedicated resources and a secretariat to facilitate this cooperation. All project informants unanimously agreed that ICMPD, with its extensive knowledge and experience in the ECOWAS region, as well as its expertise in developing resources, tools, and platforms to promote free movement, mobility, and safety (incl. the Rabat Process), was the ideal organization to facilitate this partnership.
According to all interview respondents (n=6) and emphasized during the focus group session, the thematic workstream approach ensured that the broader approach to combating TIP was designed in an interdisciplinary manner, involving and leveraging the expertise of representatives from a variety of government departments and divisions. The decision to establish sub-committees based on each thematic area was made due to the dynamic and cross-cutting nature of TIP, which affects multiple government departments and agencies. This approach recognizes the need to address TIP comprehensively and holistically, taking into consideration its multidimensional aspects that cut across various areas of governance. Reflecting a participatory consultative process, the JTWG grew from 10 initial members to 13, which now also includes representation from NGOs.
Overall, the evaluators note the high degree of engagement between various internal and external stakeholders throughout the project planning and implementation phases. This has allowed a relatively high level of motivation to participate amongst participants from both agencies, despite notable structural differences between their policy frameworks, institutional purviews and operations. While structural and contextual challenges exist between the two country contexts (incl. language differences, degree to which civil society is involved in combating TIP, differences in enforcement and judicial systems, and constraints resources dedicated to the agencies, etc.), these differences did not undermine the interest or level of engagement of participants.
Examples of ways gender pluralism, equity and human rights were considered and incorporated into the project
The NG-NR project team and core partners have, whenever possible, incorporated considerations for gender inclusion when planning the content and learnings covered across the resulting frameworks and/or products. In the development of project frameworks, such as the standard operating procedure (SOP) for the bilateral referral mechanism (BRM), informants described the incorporation of equity-related themes. For example, under the section “Ethical and Legal Considerations”, the SOP makes specific reference to gender pluralism, victim-centered and trauma informed approaches, psychosocial supports and human rights (incl. specific provisions for women and children/unaccompanied minors, persons with disabilities, etc.). Moreover, the Protections Sub-Committee, specifically, has created guidelines promoting human rights, gender sensitive protocol and specific provisions for persons with disabilities. Front-line actors, including civil society and medical staff, were also trained throughout project implementation to better address human rights concerns when protecting VOTs. Members also noted that the local language proficiencies were leveraged when implementing activities in communities to address challenges associated with literacy levels.
The JTWG's terms of reference (TOR) contain clauses that specifically emphasize gender representation and non-discrimination. Informants (n=2) express optimism that the inclusion of these principles within the operational frameworks will lead to their adherence during implementation by front-line actors. Furthermore, the expertise provided by ICMPD colleagues internally ensures that institutional policies related to these principles are effectively incorporated into the project outputs, promoting gender equality and non-discrimination in the project's activities.
The informants reported on the visibly lower female-to-male ratio among representatives of the ANLTP/TIM agency compared to NAPTIP. While gender mainstreaming has been described as an ongoing priority and consideration across both agencies, institutional gender ratio difference in recruitment and retention remains a significant challenge in ensuring gender parity (i.e., according to the Year One Report, composition of both countries’ public service sector is heavily represented by men: 69 percent in Nigeria and 84 percent in Niger). In terms of the operational work of the JTWG and sub-committees, members from both countries expressed the importance of promoting gender representation in the joint structure future-forward.
The importance of promoting a gender lens in the work of the JTWG was highlighted by members, as the project was launched in part based on the findings of the FMM West Africa study that assessed the experiences of VOT women in Agadez, where a significant majority originated from Nigeria. The study, conducted in 2017, revealed that 73 percent of VOTs rescued in Niger were from Nigeria. This underscores the need to take into account the gender dimension and address the specific vulnerabilities and challenges faced by women in the context of human trafficking within the project's activities.
The initial proposal and the results monitoring framework (RMF) of the project included plans for an extensive gender assessment during the inception phase, with the aim of developing gender-sensitive indicators for the project. Additionally, the baseline assessment referenced that data collected during the project would be disaggregated by gender, women-specific indicators would be used to assess project objectives, and gender equity would be monitored, evaluated, and reported on throughout the project. The project also aimed to counteract the marginalization of women and ensure their adequate representation and participation in all activities, including capacity-building activities and conferences with dedicated sessions on gender pluralism.
However, there is no indication that detailed gender indicators were systematically included in the updated work plans of the sub-committees or in the broader RMF of the project (albeit members of the sub-committees demonstrated consideration for gender parity during trainings/events - while this data was not captured in attendance list, attention was given to the proportion of women attending these trainings/events). This suggests a potential gap in incorporating gender-specific indicators and measures into the project's monitoring and evaluation framework and sub-committee work plans, which may need further attention to ensure effective gender mainstreaming and the promotion of gender equality in the project's implementation.
Early Indication of Project Outcomes Summary of OutcomesDescription Joint investigations and prosecutions leading to perpetrator convictionsFocus group participants have noted that the project has already enabled increased capacity to launch discreet investigations and prosecutions as well as preliminary plans for joint sting operations that require cross-border cooperation. They expect that the number of perpetrator convictions will continue to increase over time due to several factors. Firstly, improved communication between cross-border counterparts has been facilitated through the project, which has enhanced coordination and cooperation between the two agencies. Secondly, trainings on prosecution have been made available to personnel from both countries, which has contributed to their capacity to effectively investigate and prosecute cases of trafficking. Lastly, access to human and material resources has supported the implementation of protection measures for VOTs and informants.
The Investigation & Prosecution Sub-Committee has reported that efficiencies are already evident in identifying suspects and perpetrators outside their jurisdiction due to information sharing. This has led to improvements in arrests and in extraditions. BRM SOP leading to improvements in protection for VOTsThe two agencies have already begun cooperating in a more formalized manner in the identification and assistance offered to VOTs through the project's BRM SOP. This demonstrates the positive impact of the project in facilitating cross-border cooperation and enhancing the capabilities of the two agencies in combating TIP. It is expected that these efforts will contribute to increased and improved protection for VOTs and informants in the future.
Informants have shared that already there has been more rapid and efficient coordination of VOTs from both sides, this has been done outside the activities measured by the NG-NR team. Awareness raising amongst agencies and communities will increase TIP reportingThe members of the NG-NR project team emphasize the importance of increasing border capacities along corridors where there are higher rates of TIP. They note that the establishment of frameworks for cooperation, such as the MOU and JTWG/sub-committee structures, as well as border sensitization efforts for local communities, will contribute to increased information sharing across counterpart agencies and improved identification and reporting of VOTs and TIP cases.
The border sensitization efforts for local communities can also play a crucial role in preventing TIP and promoting information sharing. By raising awareness about the criminality and complexity of TIP among local communities living in areas along migratory corridors, the project can empower community members to be vigilant and report suspicious activities or cases of trafficking they may come across. This can include providing information about the services, supports, and protection measures available to VOTs, so that individuals are aware of their rights and the available resources for assistance. Improved evidence-base on TIP to inform the design of programmes, policies and legislationThe informants believe that improvements in data sharing and standardization efforts can contribute to the use of evidence-based data on TIP across the migratory corridor. This can directly improve the design of programmes and policies aimed at addressing trafficking, as well as provide a more nuanced understanding of the changing nature of TIP.
For example, by sharing data and standardizing data collection methods, the NG-NR project can create a comprehensive and reliable database of information on trafficking trends, patterns, and characteristics in the region. This data can be used to identify gaps, trends, and areas of concern, and inform the development of evidence-based interventions and policies to effectively combat trafficking. It can also help in monitoring the impact and effectiveness of existing interventions and identifying areas that may require further attention or adjustments. Lastly, it also can facilitate better coordination and collaboration among stakeholders, including government agencies, NGOs, and international organizations, by providing a common understanding of the problem and its magnitude. A number of informants (n=4) and focus group participants emphasized that the benefits of the project will translate to longer-term impact that necessitates ongoing engagement through a formalized process (e.g., a second phase of the project). While the project has resulted in an increase in trust amongst the agencies, funding and dedicated resources are needed to maintain the current momentum between the two national agencies. One informant noted that: “There will be no lasting impact at the VOT-level if there is no follow-up after this project to continue solidifying the existing benefits. The project has built a good foundation through the official establishment of cooperation frameworks, but it needs to translate further into policy and programming within each country. This process requires funding and additional facilitation and assistance from a secretariat, like ICMPD.”
KEY FINDINGS AND LESSONS LEARNED The following list of key findings and lessons learned were developed through the final evaluation process, which concluded in April 2023. However, it is important to note that the project team was granted an additional 3-month NCE following the completion of the final evaluation in April 2023. During this time, between May 2023 – June 2023, additional progress toward the project results were achieved. These achievements were reported to the evaluators but were not included in the data collection and analysis process for the final evaluation. As such, the evaluation findings, lessons learned and recommendations are based on the project’s progress until April 2023.
Figure 8. Key Findings and Lessons Learned by Criteria Area Criteria AreaKey Findings and Lessons Learned Relevance●The NG-NR project was highly relevant in both its design and implementation for project beneficiaries. The evaluators believe that the project team benefited from shared expertise across other TIP-related interventions in the ECOWAS region and through a needs assessment process at the inception of the project. The evaluators note that the project was designed in a process-oriented manner to create opportunities for national actors to lead activities and to learn from one another. ●Consultative and oversight mechanisms between the NG-NR project team and the donor resulted in a functional and effective feedback loop. The project further aligns with a number of priorities outlined by the Kingdom of Netherlands, including agreements focused on irregular migration management across West Africa. As described by representatives from the Kingdom of Netherlands, the project provides a pilot model or “blueprint” for collaboration that, if successful, can be championed across other corridors. ●The consultative needs assessment process with the two TIP agencies and the baseline assessment supported the project design, and the design of the JTWG’s structure and operations. The four thematic areas, reflecting the work of the four sub-committees (i.e., Investigation & Prosecution, Prevention, Protection & Repatriation and Partnership & Resource Mobilization), were strategically selected by the agencies due to their relevance in addressing TIP and building cohesion amongst the two agencies. The project activities under each sub-committee were intentionally developed to cover several operational priorities: trainings offered to front-line actors, capacity-building through the development of cooperation frameworks, awareness raising amongst communities, planning for longer-term sustainability, and encouraging joint-security operations – to name a few. ●The project team incorporated aspects of gender, equity and human rights considerations where possible. For example, there were specific provisions under the BRM SOP that promoted human rights, gender sensitive protocols and provisions of services for vulnerable migrants. The project M&E plan, RMF and the sub-committee work plans could be enhanced for future phases of the project to ensure that there are specific targets and indicators that correspond with these principles. Lastly, while gender mainstreaming has been described as an ongoing priority and consideration across both agencies, institutional gender ratio difference in recruitment and retention remains a significant challenge in ensuring gender parity Coherence●There is a high level of synergy with relevant interventions due to ICMPD’s position as an implementing partner with relevant projects in the region (both internal and external; e.g., FMM West Africa, OCWAR-T, etc.). ICMPD developed and leveraged its strong networks in Nigeria and Niger to ensure that they remained aware of ongoing TIP-related interventions. ●ICMPD was considered the most relevant actor to facilitate and manage the NG-NR project. The team’s knowledge of TIP within the West African context, their role as a neutral consensus broker on migration themes, and previous work on projects of similar thematic scope, collectively supported trust-building and engagement for government stakeholders. ●There was no evidence of duplication found through the evaluation process. Informants noted that ICMPD's role in developing frameworks for joint coordination and facilitating partnership-building activities between national agencies was particularly unique, as previous efforts in this regard had not materialized and the respective agencies had limited knowledge or awareness of each other's mandates and jurisdictions. ●Incorporating broader international and regional frameworks, with specific references to objectives, guidelines, standards and recommendations, into the NG-NR project documentation may support a more streamlined approach consistent with other global efforts to eradicate TIP (e.g., GCM Objectives, SDG Targets, etc.) Effectiveness●The NG-NR project was somewhat effective in achieving its planned results (13 of the 19 planned results were achieved) by the completion of the final evaluation in May 2023. Limitations in achieving results were associated with various factors; delays due to Seat Agreement requirements with Niger, turnover and recruitment barriers for the project manager role, the COVID-19 pandemic, the coup-d’état in Niger were among some of the most notable hindrances (as captured in 5.4 Efficiency). However, by securing the additional 3-month NCE, the project team was able to achieve 17 of the 19 planned indicators by June 30, 2023. ●The sub-committee's accomplishments and advancements are noteworthy, although they have also been limited in scope based on the short timeline for the project. All progress made so far is delicate and must be solidified over the long term, as the NG-NR project has been implemented in a short period with changes in institutional frameworks, practices, and people's attitudes being slow processes. ●Differential results: evaluation informants noted that due to the structural differences and capacities between NAPTIP and ANLTP/TIM, NAPTIP would likely have more capacity to advance project progress internally where applicable while ANLTP/TIM would garner more learnings through their involvement in the project and strengthened connection to NAPTIP. ●M&E processes to track the effectiveness for secondary beneficiaries (i.e., VOTs) was limited due to the lack of baseline data available and the inability to determine the extent to which the NG-NR project contributed to an increase in identified VOTs during the project period. Improved data collection processes and the standardization of data points and datasets will likely aid this process over time. Efficiency●Project resources were somewhat sufficiently converted into results. Internal and external factors related to the COVID-19 pandemic, delays in the hiring of a project manager and regulatory challenges (i.e., confirmation of necessary agreements to launch the project in both countries) resulted in activities being delayed toward the end of the project (See Figure 6: Project Challenges and Constraints). However, the project’s core team, consisting of a small number of ICMPD staff members, were able to achieve results despite the limited human resources available during the project. Leveraging internal and external resources efficiently ●As this was the first phase of the project, the evaluators noted the high degree of finish-to-start dependency between the initial activities in place to create the necessary engagement between the two agencies (e.g., establishing the JTWG and sub-committee structures under formal frameworks). Given that these frameworks are now established, activity implementation will likely progress more efficiently in future phases of the project. ●Government beneficiaries noted that the project had a high degree of buy-in from both leading agencies due to their collective goals and vision in eradicating TIP. The informants have acknowledged that there were planning, implementation, and management challenges during the NG-NR project, but they view these challenges as critical learning opportunities for future project activities. ●As of July 2023, the NG-NR team spent EUR 1,487,626.63 out of a total grant amount of € 1,590,945 (budget variance is -6%) by the end of the evaluation period. Undispersed funds were associated with the delay in hiring a project manager and with the cancellation of the Agadez field mission component of the 6th JTWG meeting due to security concerns. Impact●The NG-NR project is perceived to have a substantial and potentially expansive impact by informants. The evaluation interviewees and the focus group participants indicated that: oThe project can have a longer-term positive impact on strengthening the institutional response to TIP through enhanced bilateral cooperation. oThe benefits of NG-NR will have the potential to last and even expand to new beneficiaries, depending on how activities are streamlined across both national actors and across other migratory corridors (i.e., as a blueprint for improved partnerships in combating TIP) oDue to the significant social and human impact of TIP in Niger and Nigeria, projects such as NG-NR are needed on a longer-term and larger scale across the corridor. ●Evaluation informants noted that there have been positive results in the efficiency and effectiveness of information sharing between contacts across the two national TIP agencies (E.g., both agencies have an increased understanding of their neighbouring counterpart, new channels of communication will likely be used to share information and best practices, and organize joint activities to inquire about solutions to everyday challenges related to combating TIP) ●Significant milestones achieved through the project that are foreseen to have positive mid-to-long term outcomes are: oThe MOU providing a formalized framework for cooperation between NAPTIP and ANLTP oJoint investigations and prosecutions leading to perpetrator convictions oThe creation of the BRM SOP, leading to improvements in protection for VOTs oAwareness raising amongst agencies and communities, which is expected to increase TIP reporting, including through sensitization efforts for local communities oImproved evidence-base on TIP will inform the design of programmes, policies and legislation in the future ●The project has contributed to relationship building between the two TIP agencies. However, as consistently mentioned by informants, more funding and dedicated resources are needed to maintain the current momentum. Sustainability●The NG-NR project team has demonstrated a commitment to sharing lessons learned throughout the project implementation with project beneficiaries, ICMPD counterparts and across other interventions of similar scope via beneficiary consultations, the dedicated participatory focus group on lessons learned during the 6th JTWG meeting, meeting reports and sub-committee reports. These reports were shared with key project stakeholders, including the donor, ensuring transparency and accountability. ●A similar model that prioritizes national ownership in project interventions is a good practice that should be promoted, as it ensures that there is local capacity and commitment to sustain the benefits of the project even after its completion. The evaluators found that this principle was prioritized throughout the design of all project components and in the approach adopted for the project's execution. Moreover, the inclusion of civil society actors ensures that complementary initiatives are scaled and that duplication of programmes and services is minimized. ●Evaluation informants emphasized the need for sustained funding and a second phase of the project to ensure that the benefits achieved through the project are promoted and enhanced. Key examples of work that will be needed to sustain project benefits include: oDeveloping and implementing tangible plans to effectively operationalize and institutionalize the BRM SOP. oDeveloping and integrating BRM standards within national VOT referral mechanisms and capacity-building trainings for relevant authorities. oCreating a list of potential donors/funders and a roadmap for engaging with them. oImproving communication resources and material that highlight key results and achievements of the NG-NR project, which can be shared across government institutions, with potential donors, and with community members. oEstablishing a common center for victim assistance across the two countries to streamline resources and efforts from both agencies. oDeveloping a common database to share up-to-date data on victims and perpetrators, including information on return, readmission and reintegration. oPrioritizing additional resources and monitoring for socio-psychological and economic integration. oContinuing sensitization campaigns with local communities through conventional media and social media as a project priority, especially providing information on ways to identify TIP and prevent vulnerabilities at the border regions. oContinuing ongoing trainings, especially for law enforcement, judicial officials, medical personnel and shelter personnel, and incorporating a Training of Trainers (ToT) methodology in the training programs to ensure sustainability across institutions. oEnsuring that the DG representatives of NAPTIP and ANLTP/TIM have an in-depth understanding and familiarity with their respective counterpart agencies, as well as the needs, mandates, and activities of all sub-committees
RECOMMENDATIONS
●Sustaining communication, cooperation and coordination (CCC): continuation of the JWTG meetings will be important for future project phases so this mechanism for CCC can be further established. Doing so will better facilitate enhanced effectiveness of the sub-committees work planning and execution toward the overarching goal of better cross-border cooperation to prevent and manage TIP. ICMPD will need to play a pivotal role as a convener of this dialogue to ensure its sustainability after the project closure. The JTWG, as a CCC platform, will also better support the sustainability of frameworks produced through the NG NR projects, such as the MOU and the BRM SOP. The extent to which these frameworks will promote continued engagement amongst the two national agencies is inconclusive at this time, with informants emphasizing the need to continue fostering this engagement and the necessity of future funding sources. oTo help foster CCC amongst representatives from the two national TIP agencies, ICMPD should continue prioritizing language accessibility to ensure that their engagement in future phases is sustained (e.g., securing a flexible budget line for interpretation and translations).
●Maintaining coherence with other TIP-related interventions: the project team should continue their use of coordination and consultation mechanisms to leverage synergy opportunities across counter-trafficking actors in the region. ICMPD’s networks and involvement in relevant initiatives contributed significantly to the internal and external coherence of the project – an approach which should be adopted for the success of future phasing. At the same time, the lessons learned and good practices developed through the NG-NR project (e.g., The JTWG and sub-committee model) should be shared as a blueprint for other partnerships focused on bilateral cooperation. Lastly, incorporating broader international and regional frameworks, with specific references to objectives, guidelines, standards and recommendations, into the NG-NR project documentation may support a more streamlined approach consistent with other global efforts to eradicate TIP (e.g., GCM Objectives, SDG Targets, etc.)
●Establishing a feasible project schedule and timeline: it may be beneficial if there are future phases of the NG-NR project to plan for a longer project timeline, from the project onset (rather than requiring NCEs). This would allow for buffer time in the event of unexpected challenges (i.e., staff turnover and recruitment, political unrest) and would alleviate the resulting capacity constraints within the ICMPD team. Given the context of the region, appropriate risk planning associated with risks of project delays due to political unrest should include the incorporation of implementation buffer time, if possible. In addition, to avoid project delays, it is recommended that project plans limit start-to-finish dependencies between activities. This will prevent or mitigate the cascading effect of delays across activities, in the event that one or some activities are delayed.
●Ensuring that there are sufficient human resource allocations prior to the project launch, if possible: this could prevent, or limit project delays caused by recruitment timelines in advance of the project implementation period. This includes human resources available to the JTWG, based on the agreed upon work plans. The JTWG will need to ensure that the work required to support planned activities are not underestimated nor do they exceed project budget allocations. One good practice highlighted by informants is the NG-NR project team’s access to ICMPD’s in-house resources, for example the two thematic specialists in TIP, which enabled the allocation of supports to different components of the project, such as the development of the MOU and the BRM SOP.
●Accounting for high costs associated with travel and in-person meetings: The NG-NR team and those leading other similar interventions should remain mindful of the variable costs associated with in-person meetings. Despite in-person meetings incurring the largest percentage of project costs, they remained critical for partnership-building and virtual activities are not advised as alternatives, given internet connection issues. Additional costs to be mindful of include costs associated with travel insurance for delegates, costs to coordinate infrequent and complicated flight options between Nigeria and Niger and those associated with security protocols for safe transportation. Teams leading transnational projects can benefit from coordinating flights ahead of time and establishing buffer time for any flight delays or cancellation.
●Improving M&E practices: future phases of the NG-NR project, or relevant future interventions, should develop and maintain M&E planning and tracking documents such as a project RMF and activity logframe. Additional M&E recommendations related to the project’s relevance, efficiency and effectiveness include: oIncorporating considerations on gender, equity and human rights in the project design: Further efforts to incorporate relevant metrics and targets in project planning documents (i.e., M&E planning and tracking documents) would support better mainstreaming of these on these cross-cutting themes during project implementation, by both ICMPD and the JTWG sub-committees. oThe project team should consider outcome and impact-level indicators within their RMF. A manageable and agreed upon number of outcome and impact measures and associated indicators can support ICMPD and agency capacity improvements to track and report on project benefits over a longer period. Focus group participants also shared the importance of incorporating VOTs, migrants and community members as indirect or secondary beneficiaries, with specific data collection tools that can assess if the project is benefiting them. oThe evaluators also encourage improved standardization and alignment across indicators (i.e., clear alignment between the project’s overall RMF, sub-committee tasks as well as relevant national strategic plans related to TIP). This process can be aided by having a dedicated session at the onset of a new phase or intervention focused specifically on developing coherent sub-committee RMFs. oAs the Partnerships & Resource Mobilization Sub-Committee is responsible for sustainability of resources and funding, they can support through a more active “M&E” role, with clear considerations on how the project results are coherent and in alignment across all necessary project plans, national strategies and policies, or action plans. Alternatively, the project team may consider procuring M&E specialists to actively support the development and implementation of M&E mechanisms and processes. Either approach can help ensure that the project continuously adheres to the corresponding M&E plan. oAs the project informants noted the importance of the evaluation of the project, and specifically the opportunity to collaboratively take stock of lessons learned and key findings, the project team will benefit from ensuring that there is sufficient allocation of funds to the project’s overall evaluation, including a mid-term evaluation, but especially a final evaluation. If an in-person focus group component is preferred amongst beneficiaries, the team should consider the additional costs associated with travel and stay. oMid-term evaluation plans should be conducted at the midpoint of the project to ensure that key findings and lessons learned can shape or change management efforts with enough time to do so. oAs part of the project’s M&E management, a lengthier external institutional audit or gap analysis can be conducted to examine any changes to procedures that are in place across each national TIP agency. This assessment can serve to support reporting on how each sub-committee is addressing or meeting the recommendations provided in the audit, on a periodic basis.
●Organizing a kick-off meeting that covers operational requirements for project implementation: a clearer outline of the available budgetary spending at the beginning of the project phase can ensure that there are shared expectations of what is feasible in terms of budget allocations. In addition, this meeting can include broader discussions around financial planning that would be necessary at the onset of a new phase, such as discussions on available spending, capacity-building supports with financial reporting and supporting documentation, and other relevant topics. As mentioned earlier, the facilitating team can also utilize this opportunity to work with the sub-committees to develop results-based targets and indicators for each activity in the work plan. This kick-off meeting can serve as a crucial starting point to align expectations, ensure efficient budget utilization, and establish clear targets for the project implementation.
●Schedule meetings in advance using a shared calendar to ensure regular implementation of activities: this approach would help mitigate challenges related to coordinating on-site meetings, which currently require a lengthy back-and-forth process to find mutually available dates for participants. Additionally, each governmental institution involved in the project should designate a focal contact for administrative purposes who actively supports the planning of JTWG correspondence, including scheduling meetings. This would streamline communication and coordination, leading to more efficient and effective event planning. By proactively scheduling meetings and designating focal contacts, the JTWG can overcome logistical challenges, reduce delays, and ensure smooth coordination among project stakeholders for successful implementation.
●Sustaining project benefits: to ensure that the benefits of the NG-NR project are sustained and enhanced, evaluation informants noted that the following activities would be of most notable priority: oJTWG Informants emphasized the need to create a list of potential donors/funders and a roadmap for engaging with them, to highlight why the project requires further phases and to secure necessary funding. oA similar model that prioritizes national ownership in project interventions should be adopted for future phases of NG-NR or similar interventions. This approach better ensures that there is local capacity and commitment to sustain the benefits of the project after its completion. The evaluators found that this principle was prioritized throughout the design of all project components and in the approach adopted for the project's execution. Moreover, the inclusion of civil society actors ensures that complementary initiatives are scaled and that duplication of programmes and services is minimized. oThe regulations and protocols established through the frameworks developed under the NG-NR project, including the BRM SOP, create a standard for governmental accountability. However, evaluation informants also believe that it will be necessary to develop action plans outlining which activities and outputs will be integrated into their existing institutions if a second phase of the project does not commence. More specifically, the teams should consider: ▪Developing and implementing tangible plans to effectively operationalize and institutionalize the BRM SOP. ▪Developing and integrating BRM standards within national VOT referral mechanisms and capacity-building trainings for relevant authorities. oEstablishing a common center for victim assistance across the two countries would support efforts to streamline resources and efforts from both agencies. oDeveloping a common database to share up-to-date data on victims and perpetrators, including information on return, readmission and reintegration would enhance efficiencies in coordination between the two countries. oPrioritizing additional resources and monitoring for socio-psychological and economic integration of those who are returned would mitigate future vulnerabilities and patterns of re-migration. oContinuing coordinating sensitization campaigns with local communities through conventional media and social media, especially providing information on ways to identify TIP and prevent vulnerabilities at the border regions could contribute to increased reporting of perpetrators and assistance for VOTs. oContinuing ongoing trainings, especially for law enforcement, judicial officials, medical personnel and shelter personnel, and incorporating a ToT methodology in the training programs would support sustainability across relevant government institutions. Addressing high staff turnover across specific departments or divisions has been identified as a challenge, and training of operational or managerial level stakeholders on the harmonized BRM SOP is still needed to ensure its streamlined integration in current referral practices. oIt is important to ensure that the DG representatives of NAPTIP and ANLTP/TIM have an in-depth understanding and familiarity with their respective counterpart agencies, as well as the needs, mandates, and activities of all sub-committees, and can comfortably speak to the progress across future phases of the NG-NR project. A suggested solution from JTWG members included the representation of DGs across all subcommittees. oDeveloping a communication resource that highlights key results and achievements of the NG-NR project, can better support institutionalization of produced frameworks across relevant agencies. In addition, this resource can be shared with potential donors, and with community members to enhance buy-in and impact, respectively.
